docs.title: Health insurance renewal: 5 key numbers you should review every year
docs.text:
Are you looking to renew your health insurance policy? Do you know that when renewing your health insurance policy, it is vital to recheck several fundamentals of your policy to ensure you are adequately protected, that the policy still adds meaningful value to your life, and that it provides the health protection you need? 
 This is because renewing health insurance involves more than just paying the premium before the due date. The individual health insurance policyholder should diligently review recent changes in medical costs, any amendments to policy terms, and their current financial condition and personal circumstances, as these factors, when taken holistically, can impact both the adequacy of individual coverage and the amount paid under a claim. 
 Therefore, before renewing, keep these core fundamentals in mind and review 5 critical metrics/ numbers to determine whether your policy continues to provide adequate financial protection. 
 This metric determines the maximum coverage available to an individual. It is subject to policy terms and applicable limits. A cover that was adequate a few years ago might fall short today, as hospitalisation costs continue to rise. That is why you should review your coverage against potential treatment costs in your city and increase it if necessary. 
 To ensure a correct decision in individual cases, it is wise to seek guidance from a certified health professional and a financial advisor. This way, your policy decision will align with professional insights in a meaningful way. 
 You should also check and compare the renewable premium with last year’s payment. See how it has changed and evolved. Premiums may also increase or change due to age-related pricing, insurer rate revisions, or changes in coverage. If you find a noticeable difference, understand the reason for it, and also compare alternatives without overlooking differences in assured benefits, waiting periods, and exclusions. 
 Once you are done with the basics, you should also check whether your policy specifies any daily room rent or restricts the category of room you can opt. Check for any amendments or changes in the offered rooms. 
 This is because, in case the requirement arises, you should not be in for a surprise, and exceeding the permitted limit might also result in proportionate deductions on associated expenses, depending entirely on the policy terms . Make sure that the limit is practical and adequate for hospitals in your particular area. 
 When a company wants the policyholder to bear a specified percentage of an admissible claim, they introduce a ' co-payment clause ’ in health insurance policies. For example, with a 20% co-payment on an eligible claim of ₹ 2 lakh, the individual policyholder's share will be ₹ 40,000. Whereas the remaining ₹ 1.60 lakh will be paid by the insurer, subject to other policy terms and conditions. That is why you should carefully check whether your policy includes this clause and whether it changes at certain ages or under specific policy coverage circumstances. 
 Do not renew your health insurance policy, presuming that the terms applicable last year are going to apply in exactly the same manner this year as well. In case of doubt, speak to the customer service executive of your health insurance policy provider. 
 ‘Deductible’ is yet another important metric that needs to be rechecked. This is the amount you must bear before the insurer steps in to start paying eligible expenses under the relevant coverage. This is particularly important for super top-up policies, which generally cover eligible expenses above a specified deductible, subject to their terms. Make sure that in your case, the deductible remains reasonable for your base policy and financial capability. 
 In summary, two additional checks must be performed before the final renewal of an ongoing health insurance policy. You should also check your pre-existing diseases, waiting periods, and specific treatments, along with any accumulated no-claim bonus (NCB). 
 The network of hospitals covered by your policy should also be cross-checked, as the lists are updated regularly. A careful review of these core aspects can help an individual avoid unpleasant surprises when making a claim. 
 Disclaimer: This article is for general information only and should not be considered insurance or financial advice. Policy terms, coverage, exclusions and claim settlements vary by insurer and policy. Read your policy documents carefully and consult your insurer or a qualified advisor before making renewal decisions.

Global 
 Iran-backed militants are tightening the screws on Saudi Arabia’s crown prince
 Summer Said , Georgi Kantchev , The Wall Street Journal 7 min read 12 Oct 2026, 06:47 AM IST 
 Summary
 Mohammed bin Salman is now caught by an economy weakened by heavy spending and miscalculations of the Houthi threat. 
 Gift this article Check your portfolio 
 This is a Mint Premium article gifted to you.
Subscribe to enjoy similar stories.
 Subscribe now 
 DUBAI—Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman started the year on a high note. He had just visited the White House where he was embraced by President Trump. Even after the war with Iran kicked off, Saudi Arabia looked relatively well positioned. It could export oil through a pipeline that bypassed the blocked Strait of Hormuz.
 But the Saudis’ escalating fight with Iran-backed Houthi militants in neighboring Yemen now poses new challenges to the kingdom’s security and the crown prince’s ambitious but already struggling plans to transform the country’s oil-dependent economy.
 On Saturday, at least one Houthi missile slammed into the Saudi capital’s international airport, killing at least 12 people and injuring hundreds more, many seriously. It was the single deadliest attack on the U.S. or its Gulf allies in the conflicts related to the Iran war. A 28-year-old Egyptian flight attendant bled to death after her arm was blown off, one of several victims to lose limbs, officials briefed on the attack said.
 Two terminals were struck and their roofs partially collapsed, people familiar with the damage said. Video verified by Storyful, which like The Wall Street Journal is owned by Dow Jones, showed passengers rolling suitcases past a trail of blood on the floor as the airport was evacuated. Authorities reported more attacks on the closed airport Sunday, saying a projectile caused a fire in Terminal 4 and led to injuries.
 As recently as this summer, Saudi officials briefed journalists that the Houthi situation was under control. But the militants’ escalating attacks, which they say are retaliation for Saudi actions against them, have hit airports and energy facilities—including the kingdom’s main east-west pipeline and refineries—showing the growing threat along the southern border.
 The conflict is jeopardizing Saudi efforts to build travel and tourism into a pillar of the economy, including a marquee international investment conference scheduled for the end of the month that is now increasingly in doubt. The costs of the war have already widened the budget deficit and threaten to push the economy into contraction.
 How Prince Mohammed handles this test will have consequences that stretch well beyond the kingdom. Saudi Arabia is a major source of funding for the global tech industry and artificial intelligence projects. It is also a crucial provider of basing and overflight rights to the U.S. military.
 Trump told reporters over the weekend that the U.S. was in communication with the Houthis but might join Saudi strikes on the militant group. “What they did was very bad,” the president said Saturday night.
 On Sunday, a Houthi military spokesman reiterated the group’s warning that Saudi airports are targets. Saudi officials said they are running low on interceptors needed to fend off further strikes.
 Intensifying attacks on Riyadh, which is 500 or more miles from Houthi territory in Yemen, have transformed parts of the Saudi capital into a battle zone, with residents taking cover as explosions ring out across the city. Debris from an intercepted ballistic missile hit a kindergarten and a medical clinic complex Thursday. Workers in the city’s financial district, students at some international schools and diplomats were ordered to evacuate or take shelter.
 The 41-year-old crown prince is shuttling between heavily guarded palaces equipped with bunkers and is guarded by a handpicked security team, officials familiar with his movements said. His last public appearance was Tuesday, when he gave blood to support a national donation drive.
 The Saudi leader has few good options, said Kristian Coates Ulrichsen, a Persian Gulf expert and fellow with Rice University’s Baker Institute. “Any military response risks getting drawn in deeper to an asymmetric conflict in which the Houthis have shown they have the ability to inflict significant and symbolic damage.”
 Saudi press officials didn’t respond to a request for comment. Prince Mohammed has plowed funds over the past decade into a slate of projects with extraordinarily complex engineering requirements aimed at signaling the kingdom’s modernization and drawing investment and tourism. They include the futuristic city of Neom, an enormous cube-shaped building in Riyadh, and a desert ski resort. The total cost ran to the trillions of dollars, aggressive for a government with an annual budget of around $350 billion. The costs and economic damage of war with Iran are making that already implausible math impossible to balance.
 Foreign investment fell in the first two quarters of the year and is running well behind the crown prince’s 2030 target. Rising defense and infrastructure costs threaten to siphon away money needed for the economic diversification drive. Even the kingdom’s push to become an AI hub now carries new risks, with data centers emerging as targets.
 Many of the enormous projects spearheaded by Prince Mohammed are stalled or under review. In January, Saudi Arabia gave up on plans to host the 2029 Asian Winter Games. It still has to find a way to fund the World Expo in 2030 and the soccer World Cup four years later.
 The non-oil side of the country’s economy was smaller in the second quarter than in the first, according to Capital Economics. The Saudi Finance Ministry now expects GDP to shrink by 3.6% in 2026.
 The kingdom was able earlier in the year to pump oil across the desert to the Red Sea to escape Iran’s chokehold on the Strait of Hormuz. It got a boost from those sales and higher prices.

docs.title: Buying a ₹1 crore house? Here's the monthly salary you need to afford the home loan EMI comfortably
docs.text: Buying a ₹1 crore house involves more than arranging the down payment and securing a home loan. Buyers also need to ensure that the monthly equated monthly instalment (EMI) does not eat into their household budget, emergency savings and long-term financial goals. While a lender may approve a substantial loan based on a borrower's income and credit profile, that does not necessarily mean the borrower can comfortably afford the repayment.For a buyer making a 20% down payment of ₹20 lakh, the remaining ₹80 lakh would need to be financed through a home loan. At an illustrative interest rate of 8% a year over 20 years, the EMI would be approximately ₹66,900 a month. To manage this repayment without putting other financial priorities under pressure, the buyer would ideally need a monthly take-home salary of around ₹2.2–2.3 lakh, assuming no significant existing debt, said Sanjiv Bajaj, joint chairman and managing director of Bajaj Capital.“The first thing to look at is not just how much loan a bank is willing to offer, but how comfortably the buyer can repay it every month,” Bajaj said.How much salary do you need to buy a ₹1 crore house?The monthly income required to afford a ₹1 crore property depends on the loan amount, interest rate, repayment tenure and the buyer's existing financial commitments. A longer tenure reduces the monthly EMI but increases the total interest paid over the life of the loan.For an ₹80 lakh home loan at an illustrative interest rate of 8% a year, the EMI varies significantly depending on the repayment tenure.Bajaj recommends keeping the home loan EMI within 25-30% of monthly take-home income. This leaves room for routine household expenses, savings and unexpected financial needs.A shorter tenure helps borrowers repay the loan sooner and reduces the overall interest burden, but the higher EMI requires greater monthly income. A longer tenure offers more flexibility in the monthly budget, although the borrower pays interest over a longer period.How much interest will you pay over the loan tenure?For an ₹80 lakh loan at 8% over 20 years, total repayments would amount to approximately ₹1.61 crore, including around ₹81 lakh in interest, assuming the rate remains unchanged. Borrowers with floating-rate loans may see their EMIs or repayment tenure change as interest rates move.The choice of tenure therefore involves a trade-off between monthly affordability and the total cost of borrowing. While extending the tenure can reduce the EMI, borrowers should assess whether the additional interest is justified by the flexibility it provides.“The EMI starts becoming uncomfortable when it leaves very little room for everything else,” Bajaj said. If meeting the monthly payment requires suspending investments, relying on credit for unexpected expenses or drawing down savings, the property may be beyond the buyer's comfortable budget.What costs should homebuyers account for beyond the EMI?The down payment and monthly EMI are only part of the cost of buying a home. Buyers must also budget for stamp duty, registration, interiors, furnishing and ongoing maintenance. These expenses can substantially increase the upfront amount required to purchase a property.Using most of one's savings to fund the purchase can leave a household financially vulnerable. Buyers should retain an emergency fund and ensure that they can continue meeting other financial commitments after paying the down payment and associated charges.Another common mistake is treating a bank's loan approval as confirmation that a property is affordable. Lenders assess repayment capacity based on their own eligibility criteria, but borrowers must also account for household expenses, family responsibilities, existing loans and future financial goals.For instance, a ₹67,000 EMI may appear manageable for a buyer earning ₹2.2 lakh a month. However, the same repayment could become stressful if the buyer also has a car loan, personal loan or substantial family expenses.How can buyers avoid stretching their finances?Bajaj advises prospective buyers to work backwards from an EMI they can comfortably afford rather than start with the maximum property price a lender will finance.Buyers should assess whether they can continue their monthly investments, meet household expenses and handle unexpected medical or family costs without dipping into their savings. They should also consider whether they could continue making payments if their income were disrupted or interest rates increased.Repayment capacity can change over a 15-20-year loan tenure because of career breaks, changing family responsibilities or higher living costs. Buyers should therefore avoid basing their decisions solely on their current income and expenses.Ultimately, the right home budget is not determined solely by the loan a bank is willing to offer. It should be based on the repayment a household can sustain while maintaining its standard of living, protecting its savings and continuing to work towards other financial goals.

docs.title: How the oil crisis is morphing into a shipping crisis, in 5 charts
docs.text:
Plain Facts 
 How the oil crisis is morphing into a shipping crisis, in 5 charts
 howindialives.com 5 min read 12 Oct 2026, 07:01 AM IST 
 Summary
 Since the US-Iran war started, shipping costs have risen 8-10 times for oil, about 73% for finished goods, and about 49% for commodities. Shipowners are making higher margins and investing in new capacity, while taking on greater risk. 
 Gift this article Check your portfolio 
 This is a Mint Premium article gifted to you.
Subscribe to enjoy similar stories.
 Subscribe now 
 When Israel and the US began attacking Iran at the end of February, analysts predicted that headline oil prices would soon cross $200 a barrel. That hasn’t materialized yet. Even as the war has continued, global stock markets, driven by an AI mania, have soared. 
 But that doesn't mean there is no oil crisis. It is simmering in the background. Market experts are now warning of multiple crises. Speaking at an energy conference in London, Russell Hardy, chief executive of commodities trading giant Vitol, said that what started as a crude oil crisis became an oil products (petrol, aviation fuel) crisis, and has now morphed into a shipping crisis. 
 All at sea 
 For oil industry analysts, a shipping crisis, especially those ships trying to move crude oil and gas out of the Strait of Hormuz , is now their topmost concern. Even as the US upped its efforts to move ships through the Strait of Hormuz, Iran escalated its attacks on merchant ships braving the waterway. Numerous seamen have been killed in the attacks. The danger has also forced shipping costs up dramatically.
 The average cost of shipping 1,000 barrels of crude on the West Asia to Indian west coast route escalated from $0.5-0.6 per mile in 2022-2025 to $3.4 per mile in June 2026 and further to $5.1 per mile in August 2026. This is about 8-10 times the average from 2022 to 2025, according to data from Clarksons Research, a maritime data and research firm. According to a Hindustan Times report in September, daily charter rates for tankers to India more than doubled in two weeks as conflicts escalated in West Asia. 
 Risk and reward 
 The surge in freight rates has boosted shipowners’ earnings. Gross earnings of shipowners to ship crude in very large crude carriers (VLCCs) from West Asia to China—a benchmark route to assess freight costs—are now about $1.2 million per day, against about $480,000 in early August. Net earnings will be lower, factoring in insurance and crew incentives. 
 Higher freight rates and crude prices also give shipowners an incentive to take greater risks with their vessels and crews. Tankers willing to traverse the Strait of Hormuz now follow a ‘shuttle’ system. They pass through the Strait with their transponders, which broadcast GPS locations, switched off and under the cover of darkness.
 Their destination is the Gulf of Oman, where they offload crude to another tanker before returning for another load. The second tanker carries the crude to its final destination, whether China or India .
 Costs not contained 
 The disruption is no longer confined to oil tankers. Shipping costs for other goods, including finished products transported in standardized containers, have also risen.
 The Freightos baltic index (FBX), a global benchmark of container shipping costs, has risen 73% since the US-Iran war began. Although the latest increase is not as much as seen during the covid years of 2020 and 2021, it is still significant. Segments that are directly impacted by the war, like crude oil shipping, have seen a much faster rise. 
 One obvious reason for the rise in container freight costs is the increase in bunker fuel prices. Used to power ships, bunker fuel has become more expensive alongside other fuels because of the war. In addition, shippers have been avoiding the Red Sea routes through the Suez Canal for a few years now because of Houthi attacks in the region. Instead, they have been traversing longer routes to Europe through the Cape of Good Hope. In recent weeks, though, Suez Canal traffic has picked up, according to Bloomberg . 
 Commodity constraints 
 Transporting ‘dry bulk’ cargo, including commodities such as iron ore and foodgrain, has also become more expensive for reasons similar to those affecting container shipping. The Baltic Dry Index has risen about 49% since the US-Iran war began.
 However, multiple factors drive commodity shipping prices, not just the US-Iran war. For instance, both Russia and Ukraine are major grain exporters. Their war, since February 2022, has disrupted exports, especially in the past two months, with each attacking the other’s trade infrastructure, such as ships and ports.
 While trade data and analytics company Kpler recently noted that crude oil exports through the Strait of Hormuz have increased sharply in recent weeks, it added that the recovery did not mean a return to normal market conditions. The “continued threat to vessels transiting Hormuz is keeping freight costs elevated,” and the market was therefore demonstrating that a diplomatic solution was not necessary to restore physical supply, but operating without one came at a cost, it added. 
 Supply gains 
 If Kpler’s reading is correct, and given the dynamics of the Russia-Ukraine war as well, shipping costs will remain high for some time to come. Higher revenues for shipowners and operators mean greater incentive to invest in new shipping capacity. The year 2025 saw the maximum number of new ships built (in tonnage terms) since at least 2014, according to UN Trade and Development (UNCTAD) data. 
 Two countries, China and South Korea, dominate the global market for shipbuilding, accounting for about 80% of new shipping tonnage added in the last three years, up from 65-70% in the previous decade. More is expected to come. 
 According to the Baltic and International Maritime Council, a shipping industry association, the global shipping order book in early 2026, comprising new ships on order at shipyards

docs.title: India’s export imperative: Here’s how we must mitigate trade risks amid global turmoil
docs.text:
Opinion 
 India’s export imperative: Here’s how we must mitigate trade risks amid global turmoil
 Puja Mehra , Arpita Mukherjee 4 min read 11 Oct 2026, 04:00 PM IST 
 Summary
 As the world becomes a less reliable source of capital, India’s export earnings must rise. Although geopolitical uncertainty is beyond the Centre’s control, it still has many ways to boost exports. Here's what policymakers should consider. 
 Gift this article Check your portfolio 
 This is a Mint Premium article gifted to you.
Subscribe to enjoy similar stories.
 Subscribe now 
 For years, macroeconomic policymakers had a settled view of India’s external financing strategy. A current-account deficit could be financed by capital inflows, principally foreign direct investment and portfolio investment. The flows could change in composition and timing or prove inconvenient, but they were a dependable source of dollars beyond doubt. 
 The past two years have seen a structural break. India’s current-account deficit has remained well behaved. But capital inflows have not been sufficient. This has put pressure on the rupee. 
 The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) has had to search for dollars, including through expensive measures to attract subsidized foreign-currency deposits from non-residents, which are no substitute for a dependable source. Their costs will ultimately fall on Indian savers, borrowers and taxpayers. 
 As the world becomes a less reliable source of capital, India’s export earnings must rise. 
 RBI’s data show that merchandise exports rose from 9.7% of GDP in 2000-01 to almost 17% in 2011-12. A turn towards protectionism over the past decade has left India a larger economy without proportionate success at selling goods abroad. Merchandise exports were about 11.4% of GDP in 2025-26. 
 Merchandise exports must recover. The timing is not ideal. India cannot reopen the Strait of Hormuz. Nor can New Delhi determine what tariff the Trump administration in the US might impose next. Much of that uncertainty facing exporters is beyond the government’s control. 
 Trade-policy uncertainty doesn’t emerge only from headline tariffs. It is also created by ministry and regulatory decisions that affect exports. 
 A tariff concession negotiated in a free trade agreement (FTA) may be undermined by a compliance requirement. A quality-control order or customs duty may change the economics of a key imported input. A budget announcement may remain on paper because the administrative follow-up gets lost between ministries. 
 In 2014, the Narendra Modi government abolished the Cabinet Committee on WTO Matters. It may be time to revive the Trade and Economic Relations Committee that Prime Minister Manmohan Singh constituted in 2005. Chaired by the PM, the forum brought together India’s finance, commerce and external affairs ministers, senior economic officials and the national security advisor to coordinate the country’s external economic policy. 
 The prime minister’s office plays a similar role in other areas. Trade policy needs the same attention to ensure that trade-related budget decisions taken by the government and the follow-up needed to turn FTA commitments into export opportunities do not get lost in government machinery. 
 India’s Foreign Trade Policy of 2023 broke with the conventional five-year cycle without clarifying when the next comprehensive policy would be due. It also set a $2 trillion export goal for 2030. The government has since announced a $1 trillion export goal for 2026-27. Exporters need clarity on how these targets fit into the policy framework and the Export Promotion Mission, which has an outlay of ₹ 25,060 crore. 
 Quality control orders (QCOs), intended to raise standards, can act as non-tariff barriers. The 2026-27 budget announced their rationalization. In June, the Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade notified the Transition Facilitation (Quality Control) Order, 2026, offering an alternative compliance mechanism for some QCOs. 
 The task force could discuss whether further changes are needed and how the process can be made predictable across products and ministries. 
 There is a similar case for countervailing duties. They may be justified in particular cases, but a more systematic framework would make the policy less unpredictable for domestic producers and importers. 
 The task is not only to address current trade barriers, but to anticipate future ones. Indian exporters will increasingly face environmental, labour and other sustainability audit requirements in key markets like the EU and UK. Domestic measures such as the four labour codes and Bharat Trade Net will matter only if implemented on the ground in time to help exporters meet those requirements. 
 The 2024-25 budget announced a six-month comprehensive review of India’s customs-duty structure with the aim of simplifying and rationalizing it, eliminating duty inversion, reducing disputes and facilitating export-led trade. Some of the problems that the review was meant to address remain. 
 Imports from FTA partners, for example, may enter India at preferential or zero duty, while goods supplied by a special economic zone (SEZ) to the domestic tariff area face applicable customs duties. Where the tariff treatment does not adequately recognize value addition within the SEZ, production may face an unintended disadvantage. 
 FTAs require an even more systematic follow-through. Which agencies are the nodal points for discussing implementation with partner countries? What is being done to map skill gaps and increase exports of skilled workers? How ready are firms to meet new sustainability rules? How are the proposed mutual recognition agreements progressing? Each chapter of an FTA has commitments and areas for cooperation that need to be translated into an implementation plan. 
 Geopolitical risks are beyond our control. Avoidable uncertainty at home is not. 
 The authors are, respectively, senior fellow (consultant) and profess

docs.title: Diversifying your portfolio in the age of AI is tricky. How to do it.
docs.text:
Global 
 Diversifying your portfolio in the age of AI is tricky. How to do it.
 Barrons 4 min read 11 Oct 2026, 12:25 PM IST 
 Summary
 AI-related stocks are the main driver behind many broad indexes. And even the traditional hedge to equities—the bond market—is moving with stocks. 
 Gift this article Check your portfolio 
 This is a Mint Premium article gifted to you.
Subscribe to enjoy similar stories.
 Subscribe now 
 Diversifying your portfolio isn’t as simple as it once was.
 The artificial-intelligence boom is lifting many boats, including sectors and in regions typically driven by different fundamentals. AI-related stocks are the main driver behind many broad indexes. And even the traditional hedge to equities—the bond market—is moving with stocks.
 What can an investor do? Dive deep into your current holdings to discover what you are exposed to, experts say. Then tweak your investments by finding assets that are less correlated with each other to spread the risk.
 Here’s how.
 Take stock
 Get under the hood of your investments in your 401(k) and other investment accounts. What funds do you hold? What do those funds include? And what’s driving their returns?
 “You really have to do the X-ray and know how much they overlap and how much you are exposed to the more volatile areas of the AI trade,” said Patrick Huey, owner of Victory Independent Planning.
 Even traditionally diverse index funds need a second look.
 Many are designed to track the performance of a broad index, such as the S&P 500. But the index is capitalization weighted, meaning larger companies influence the index’s performance more. Lately, those large companies are AI ones.
 That is all well and good when those stocks are booming. But if—and when—they lead to a selloff, that leaves your portfolio overexposed to the AI trade.
 “In 401ks, you’re kind of forced into these index funds and so you’re gonna take it on the chin if the market goes down,” said Monica Dwyer, a senior vice president at Harvest Financial Advisors.
 How to diversify with U.S. stocks
 So let’s diversify—starting with U.S. stocks.
 One big factor to consider is how directly exposed a stock or sector is to the AI trade. While AI is buoying the fortunes of traditionally less correlated sectors like technology, utilities and real estate, the boost isn’t uniform.
 AI chip companies and memory chip manufacturers have the most direct exposure, whereas many areas of real estate—such as retail or multifamily—have much less.
 Power companies, the energy demand from data centers, may fall in the middle.
 “Utilities probably tend to become more correlated with technology and AI than we used to think,” said Laura Mattia, senior vice president at Wealth Enhancement.
 Then there are sectors like healthcare. While AI may eventually improve healthcare services or disease research, healthcare demand is largely driven by an aging population, a trend that continues to grow—with or without AI.
 And if you want a large-cap index fund, “focus more on an equal-weighted one,” Mattia said.
 Look for mutual funds or exchange-traded funds like Invesco S&P 500 Revenue ETF that weights companies in the S&P 500 by revenue or Invesco S&P 500 Equal Weight ETF that gives each company the exact same weighting.
 Go international
 Investing in stocks abroad won’t automatically diversify your portfolio now. U.S. equities make up roughly half of the global market, according to FactSet, and AI remains a big driver in overseas indexes.
 So examine what your international holdings actually are. If you find too much AI exposure, maybe move away from those large-cap international stocks. Consider small-cap internationals instead.
 “It’s an interesting asset class that has done very well over the recent year or two,” Mattia said. “They’re more influenced by local behavior as opposed to the global economy.”
 Fix your fixed income
 Don’t forget to pore over your less risky assets like bonds.
 “Historically you look for bonds to zig while stocks are zagging, and the reality is they’re very highly correlated recently,” said Catherine Valega, a certified financial planner at Green Bee Advisory.
 Instead, Valega is turning to stable short-term liquid alternatives such as money-market funds, U.S. Treasury bills and certificates of deposit, or CDs, to fill out the conservative portion of her clients’ portfolios.
 “ CDs are FDIC insured and Treasury bills are backed by the full faith and credit of the U.S. government, so why would I take a credit risk?” Valega said.
 For corporate bonds, check out reinsurance or catastrophic bonds, which are influenced by natural disasters—and not larger economic trends.
 “A tsunami in Asia has nothing to do with what the Federal Reserve decides at their next FOMC meeting,” Mattia said, “so there it’s just a different source of risk.”
 Think outside the box
 Maybe it’s time for some tried-and-true alternative assets—like commodities and precious metals. Take gold, for example.
 “It has almost zero correlation to the U.S. stock market,” said Matthew McKay, director of investments at Briaud Financial Advisors. “It has been a bit more correlated this past year but overall it’s a pretty noncorrelated asset.”
 As for energy commodities, consider this: When stocks went gangbusters in recent years, energy commodities “blew it out of the water when you compare it,” McKay said.
 If your 401(k) doesn’t offer a commodity fund, try a precious metals equity fund, McKay said.
 “When gold’s performing well, gold-mining stocks are like double, triple that type of performance,” he said, “so it’s a good diversifier from that perspective.”

docs.title: Struggling to monetise your art? How to earn revenue with the ‘1,000 True Fans’ theory
docs.text:
Instead of chasing audiences, it focuses on people who value your work deeply. These supporters buy your creations and help you continue making them. For independent artists, that relationship can become the foundation of a sustainable career. Kevin Kelly introduced the idea in 2008 through his essay, ‘1,000 True Fans’. He was the founding executive editor of Wired magazine. His argument was simple: creators could earn without depending on companies or fame. A true fan does more than like a post or watch a video. They buy your books, attend performances, collect prints and support new releases. They also share your work and encourage others to discover it. Their support comes from a lasting interest in what you create. Consider an artist offering a subscription at ₹ 100 per month. If 1,000 fans subscribe, the monthly revenue reaches ₹ 1,00,000. Over 12 months, that adds up to ₹ 12,00,000 in revenue. This calculation shows how smaller payments can add up through regular support. The key is finding people willing to pay consistently for something they value. A writer could offer exclusive essays or stories through a monthly subscription. A musician could share special recordings while an artist could offer creative process updates. Prints, books, performance tickets and online classes provide other ways for fans to spend. This approach changes what you measure as success. A thoughtful comment, repeat purchase or personal recommendation becomes worth your attention. You spend more energy strengthening relationships with people who are interested. You worry less about whether every post reaches a huge audience. Advertising and streaming models usually need large audiences because each view earns very little. That pressure can push creators towards attention-grabbing content instead of their own interests. Direct support allows you to focus on work your committed audience appreciates. Monthly subscriptions also offer a regular income base for planning future projects. Building a community of ‘1,000 True Fans’ takes time, consistent work and meaningful conversations. Start with a free portfolio that helps people understand your style. Share public posts, podcast episodes, artwork or short clips. Give new visitors enough material to decide whether your work interests them. Then explain clearly what paying supporters will receive. Keep the first paid option simple and useful. You can offer additional benefits through higher subscription levels. These could include signed prints, merchandise or opportunities to ask questions directly. Let supporters see how your work develops. Share rough sketches, early drafts, mistakes and lessons from your process. These glimpses can help fans feel involved in your creative journey. Respond to their interest and recognise the people already supporting you. The ‘1,000 True Fans’ theory encourages artists to build stronger connections around their work. Reaching 1,000 committed supporters will require patience and effort. But the aim is clear: create value that people want to support repeatedly. Your art can then grow through a community that wants you to keep creating. Sounak Mukhopadhyay covers trending news, sports and entertainment for LiveMint. His reporting focuses on fast-moving stories, box office performance, digital culture and major cricket developments. He combines real-time updates with clear context for everyday readers.

Sounak brings newsroom experience across breaking news, explainers and long-form features. He has a strong emphasis on accuracy, verification and responsible storytelling. His work tracks audience behaviour, celebrity influence and the business of sport and cinema. He helps readers understand why a story matters beyond the headline.

Sounak has contributed to widely read digital publications. He continues to build a body of journalism shaped by consistency, speed and editorial clarity. He is particularly interested in the intersection of media, popular culture and public conversation in contemporary India.

At LiveMint, he writes daily coverage as well as analytical pieces that interpret numbers, trends and cultural moments in accessible language. His approach prioritises factual depth, balanced framing and reader trust. The reporting aligns with modern newsroom standards of transparency and credibility.

Outside daily reporting, he explores storytelling across formats including podcasts, filmmaking and narrative non-fiction. Through his journalism, Sounak aims to document the rhythms of modern entertainment and sports while maintaining rigorous editorial integrity.

Sounak continues to develop audience-focused journalism that connects speed with substance in a rapidly-changing information environment. His work seeks clarity, trust and lasting public value in every story he reports. docs.title: Rahul Gandhi seizes the streets, but Delhi remains distant
docs.text:
Opinion 
 Rahul Gandhi seizes the streets, but Delhi remains distant
 Shashi Shekhar 4 min read 12 Oct 2026, 05:30 AM IST 
 Summary
 The Congress sees an opportunity in the changed political landscape and believes it can drive a harder bargain with regional satraps. 
 Gift this article Check your portfolio 
 This is a Mint Premium article gifted to you.
Subscribe to enjoy similar stories.
 Subscribe now 
 An unprecedented disruption swept across New Delhi and the National Capital Region on Saturday. As many as 245 trains were cancelled. More than 40 stations of the Delhi Metro were shut down. Bus routes were diverted. Many schools held online classes and some exams were cancelled. Roads were under unprecedented barricading.
 It achieved desired results. Supporters of the Cockroach Janata Party (CJP) failed to make it to Jantar Mantar. Their leader Abhijit Dipke and his associates were arrested. Through the day, the Delhi police arrested 7,000 people. Frustrated, the protesters have declared they will carry on with their resistance. It seems after a long time protests and protesters are back on Indian streets.
 But some pertinent questions need to be addressed.
 Has the sanctity of examinations been restored since Dharmendra Pradhan’s resignation ? Will chief election commissioner Gyanesh Kumar’s resignation solve all the problems? Will the protesters promise that if Gyanesh Kumar resigns, they will not launch another movement? Are these youngsters planning to form a political party and contest elections? Or they want to play the role of a pressure group?
 Let’s go back to the beginning to answer these questions.
 On Tuesday, Rahul Gandhi lead more than 200 lawmakers of the opposition INDIA bloc from Parliament gate to the Election Commission office. Police and paramilitary forces arrested them near Akashwani Bhawan. But the Congress MPs sat there for 9 hours. Rahul said the MPs were going to meet Gyanesh Kumar. The Election Commission denied any request for a meeting. The police, sensing the protest may stretch for long, rounded up everyone and dropped them at a far-off place. The next day, they arrested Priyanka Gandhi and other Congress leaders heading for Jantar Mantar. On Thursday, these people flocked to Rajghat and on Friday at Rashtrapati Bhavan. It’s interesting to note that whatever Rahul Gandhi told the media after meeting the president was denied by the Rashtrapati Bhavan staff within 90 minutes.
 It’s no coincidence that Rahul has surprised people over the last four months. He has staged a sit-in near the prime minister’s residence, appeared at the Parliament Street police station and has now taken his protests to other locations in Delhi.
 Rahul Gandhi is trying to shed the perception that he cannot take the fight to the ground. He has recognized the power of visibility, with videos of his face-off with the police going viral and garnering millions of views.
 In the coming months, five states including, Uttar Pradesh, will hold assembly elections. Though the Congress has a limited presence in Uttar Pradesh, it lost the opportunity to form a government in Goa and Meghalaya due to its own weakness. In Punjab, the Aam Aadmi Party (AAP) not only wrested power, but established itself as a strong incumbent. That’s why the Congress is in no mood to miss any opportunity.
 When in 2013 Narendra Modi made his dash towards Delhi, the Congress was unable to forcefully deny the allegations levelled against the party. Similarly, the AAP easily brushed aside Sheila Dixit’s 15 years of good work. Even in Punjab and Gujarat, the AAP has upset Congress’s applecart.
 During the July CJP protests , Rahul Gandhi sat in front of the prime minister’s residence as he didn’t want another competitor to emerge. Before the CJP’s 10 October protest, he tried hard to present himself as the lead face of the resistance.
 The AAP maintained a strategic distance from the high-voltage drama. In the coming Punjab elections, the party is in direct contest with the Congress. Then in Gujarat, the AAP wants to capitalize on the 12.92% of votes it secured in the last assembly polls. In the past, the Congress’s short-term alliances with communists and socialists have contributed to its long-term decline.
 We should look at the compulsions of the other members of the INDIA bloc. They don’t want Congress to expand in their states beyond a point. But they need its support to ward off the existential threat. Mamata Banerjee is a glaring example. Her 20 Lok Sabha and four Rajya Sabha MPs have switched sides. Tejashwi Yadav’s Rashtriya Janata Dal could win just 25 seats in the 2025 Bihar polls.
 The Congress sees an opportunity in the changed political landscape and believes it can drive a harder bargain with regional satraps. This explains Rahul Gandhi’s renewed push, with his sights set on the 2029 general election. But before taking on Narendra Modi, the party must deliver strong performances in assembly polls. I am reminded of Hazrat Nizamuddin Auliya’s famous quip: Hanoz dilli door ast . Delhi is still far off.
 Shashi Shekhar is editor-in-chief, Hindustan. Views are personal.

Global 
 Why economists think higher bond yields are here to stay
 Matt Grossman , Anthony DeBarros , The Wall Street Journal 5 min read 11 Oct 2026, 03:33 PM IST 
 Summary
 The WSJ quarterly survey reveals that forecasters think inflation, Federal Reserve rate increases and debt will keep borrowing costs higher for longer. 
 Gift this article Check your portfolio 
 This is a Mint Premium article gifted to you.
Subscribe to enjoy similar stories.
 Subscribe now 
 Some economic shocks look like bumps in the road—tariffs, to which businesses adjust, or a war with Iran that raises oil prices temporarily. But economists increasingly believe that higher U.S. interest rates will define the rest of the decade.
 So concludes The Wall Street Journal’s latest survey of forecasters. The surveyed analysts don’t see the recent surge in long-term yields to quarter-century highs as a temporary blip that will fade as inflation cools. Instead, they expect higher long-term yields to be sustained.
 Treasurys set the tempo for borrowing costs across the economy. Higher yields mean higher mortgage rates and more expensive borrowing for companies. They also increase the burden on the federal budget, where interest on the national debt now exceeds military spending.
 The 71 analysts who submitted projections in the survey from Oct. 2-7 now expect the benchmark 10-year yield to end 2026 at 5.1%, up from 4.4% the last time we asked, in July. Not all respondents answered every question.
 Higher yields are expected to persist. Forecasters see a 10-year yield of 4.96% halfway through 2027 and 4.78% at the end of 2027, up from 4.3% and 4.26% in July projections.
 A mix of improving growth, new inflationary pressures and concerns about the U.S. fiscal trajectory have pushed bond yields higher since the start of the summer. Many economists said the cocktail has forced them to re-evaluate their assumptions about investors’ demand for Treasurys, whose yields rise when their prices fall.
 “It has been a sea change in the fundamentals underlying the fixed-income market and the economy,” Allen Sinai, president of consulting firm Decision Economics, said in an interview.
 He said that even after the Federal Reserve’s first interest-rate increase in three years last month, the central bank has fallen behind in the battle to tame inflation. Sinai said it would take more than one hike to smother inflation, which the Fed appeared to acknowledge with its September projections. Those showed the Fed’s short-term interest-rate target, the federal-funds rate, topping 4% this year and staying there through 2027.
 “The fundamental sea change for me was the recognition of that by the Fed,” Sinai said. He forecasts that the 10-year yield could rise to nearly 6% next year and remain above 5% through the 2020s. Yields on Treasury securities are heavily influenced by investors’ expectations for how the Fed will set interest rates in coming years.
 The rise in yields comes despite little change in expectations for growth in gross domestic product or inflation.
 Much of the recent increase in inflation is because of higher oil prices, which economists expect to recede: They forecast that the U.S. oil-price benchmark will end the year at $88 a barrel, compared with $91.85 on Friday, and slip below $80 by July.
 As a result, they expect inflation as measured by the consumer-price index of 3.5% in December, 2.6% next June, and 2.3% at the end of 2027. That has changed little from three months ago. The inflation gauge that the Fed tracks, the personal-consumption expenditures price index, is forecast to cool to 2.4% by the end of 2027, from 3.5% at the end of this year.
 Carl Tannenbaum, chief economist at Chicago-based Northern Trust, said factors beyond the inflation outlook have pushed up expected yields.
 Inflationary pressure from the Iran war could abate if the conflict winds down, which would help ease yields, all else equal, he said. But investors will remain nervous about the large and growing U.S. debt burden, while the AI infrastructure build-out could lift growth expectations and demand for capital, Tannenbaum said. He sees the 10-year yield around 5.2% through 2028, before falling to 5% by the end of 2029.
 Yields at that level would strain the federal budget. In February, the Congressional Budget Office projected that the 10-year Treasury yield won’t exceed 4.3% for the rest of the decade. The White House Office of Management and Budget is even more optimistic, projecting yields falling into the mid-3% range later this decade.
 Economists penciled in higher expected growth this year. They now expect GDP to increase by 2.4% in 2026, up from their 2.1% July projection. That mostly reflects upward revisions to second-quarter growth and interim data suggesting the economy might have grown by an annualized rate of more than 3% in the third quarter. Survey respondents see growth slipping back thereafter, to 2.1% or 2.2% for the rest of the decade.
 Likewise, forecasters don’t anticipate much drama in the labor market. On average, they think unemployment will hang around 4.2% through 2029, little changed from the 4.2% unemployment rate in September. They put the probability of recession in the coming 12 months at 24%, barely budged from 25% in July.
 Not all forecasters agree that yields will stay high. Rajeev Dhawan, an economist at Georgia State University, thinks that the labor market is more fragile than it appears. Over the past six months, the economy has added a solid 66,000 jobs a month on average, but few have been in the most lucrative fields such as finance and tech, he said.
 In Dhawan’s view, a weaker labor market could force the Fed to reverse course and bring rates lower again in the near future, which could pull down bond yields.
 “The labor market’s got a white-collar job malaise,” Dhawan said. “Once the Fed realizes it isn’t as strong, they will pivot to rate cuts.”

Nifty's 2027 challenge: Can it outrun S&P 500 amid global mkt uncertainty?
 India's earnings growth and relatively lower trailing valuations offer hope, but foreign outflows and external risks could limit the Nifty's recovery
 premium 
 Indian equities face a test as investors weigh earnings growth and valuations against the stronger performance of US stocks.
 Pravin Palande Mumbai 4 min read Last Updated : Oct 11 2026 | 11:08 PM IST
 Listen to This Article
 Wall Street is scaling record highs, while Dalal Street struggles to regain lost ground. The Nifty 50 has fallen 11 per cent over the past year, compared with a 17 per cent return for the S&P 500, raising the question of whether Indian equities can turn the tables next year. 
 The Nifty’s 0.44 per cent gain last week ended a run of eight weekly losses, its longest losing streak in a quarter of a century. This comes at a time when the Reserve Bank of India has raised interest rates, foreign institutional investors (FIIs) are selling in October, and oil prices are high. 
 So far in October, FIIs have been net sellers of Indian equities worth ₹38,503 crore. On October 9, when the Nifty broke its losing streak, FIIs sold equities worth ₹12,884 crore. Either they do not see growth prospects in India, or they see better opportunities in the S&P 500. 
 Just three days earlier, the mood among traders in New York was euphoric. On October 6, the S&P 500 closed at an all-time high of 7,811.54, despite elevated 10-year bond yields and the ongoing Iran war. 
 Over the past year, the Nifty 50 has fallen 11 per cent, while the S&P 500 has delivered a return of 17 per cent. Will the Nifty deliver higher returns than the S&P 500 next year? 
 The answer lies in how investors view corporate earnings growth in the two markets. In India, the earnings season has begun, with Tata Consultancy Services reporting 2026-27 second-quarter (Q2FY27) net profit of ₹13,884 crore, up 15 per cent, and revenue of ₹73,188 crore, up 11 per cent. Both figures beat expectations. 
 Kotak Institutional Equities (KIE) expects the net profits of Nifty firms to rise 21 per cent in Q2FY27, with earnings per share (EPS) rising 17.9 per cent in FY27 and 13.4 per cent in FY28. “We expect Q2FY27 net profits of the Nifty 50 index to increase 21 per cent year-on-year. We estimate the EPS of the Nifty 50 index at ₹1,227 for FY27 and ₹1,398 for FY28,” KIE anaylsts wrote in a preview. 
 FactSet, a financial data and analytics company, expects S&P 500 earnings to grow 32.7 per cent in calendar year (CY) 2026 and 15.8 per cent in CY27. Based on these forecasts, Wall Street is expected to deliver faster earnings growth this year and next, rather than relying on a single strong quarter. 
 India’s earnings growth depends on automotive, banking, metal, and oil companies, which stand to benefit from stronger demand, improved margins or higher oil prices. Information technology services are expected to post profit growth of only 8 per cent. 
 By contrast, US earnings growth is being driven by artificial intelligence (AI). AI infrastructure stocks are expected to account for more than half of the S&P 500’s earnings growth this quarter, according to a report by Ben Snider, chief US equity strategist at Goldman Sachs. Nvidia Corporation and Micron Technology alone are expected to account for more than one-third of the entire index’s earnings growth. 
 “Because equity prices have failed to keep pace with surging earnings, near-term valuations show no hint of a bubble,” Snider writes. The forward price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio has fallen from 23x a year ago to 19x today, matching its 10-year average, he says. 
 That brings us to valuations. Using prices at the October 5 close, KIE values the Nifty at 18.3x its FY27 earnings and 16x its FY28 earnings. 
 Goldman Sachs puts the S&P 500 at 19.1x forward earnings. 
 Based on trailing P/E multiples, the Nifty 50, at 19.3x, looks cheaper than the S&P 500, at 26.5x. The S&P 500 is more expensive on both trailing (19.3x vs 26.5x) and forward (18.3x vs 19.1x) earnings. While, Nifty is cheaper than the S&P 500. Yet the Nifty has delivered negative returns despite corporate earnings growth. 
 For the S&P 500, the challenge is to sustain its earnings momentum. Delivering another year of strong growth may prove harder than the current forecasts suggest, particularly when compared with the earnings projections in KIE’s preview. 
 Goldman Sachs Research forecasts that the S&P 500 will rise to 8,700 over the next 12 months, from 7,764 on September 21. That implies an upside of 12.1 per cent. Ideally, the Nifty 50 will outperform that return over the coming year.

Nifty 50 trails Asian peers; Kospi and Taiex nearly double, shows data
 The Nifty 50 ranked second-last among 18 major markets over the past year, ahead only of Indonesia, Bloomberg data show
 The lag is not limited to Wall Street, where the S&P 500 rose 15.8 per cent in the past year and London’s FTSE 100 10.9 per cent
 Shilpa Rangarajan Mumbai 5 min read Last Updated : Oct 11 2026 | 11:11 PM IST
 Listen to This Article
 Indian equities have fallen behind their Asian and global peers, with the Nifty 50 ranking second-last ahead of only Indonesia among 18 major markets over the past year, Bloomberg data shows.
 The Nifty closed at 22,520.45 on Friday, down 10.6 per cent from a year earlier, days after touching an 18-month low.
 South Korea’s Kospi rose 86.7 per cent and Taiwan’s Taiex 80.6 per cent, leaving the Indian benchmark 97 and 91 percentage points behind. Only Indonesia’s Jakarta Composite, down 26.1 per cent, fared worse.
 The gap grew wider over two years, the data showed, as investors who put ₹100 in the Nifty in October 2024 now hold about ₹90. The same sum would be worth ₹255 in the Kospi, ₹218 in the Taiex, ₹176 in Japan’s Nikkei 225, ₹135 in the S&P 500, ₹128 in the London’s FTSE 100 and ₹117 in Hong Kong’s Hang Seng, in local-currency terms.
 The lag is not limited to Wall Street, where the S&P 500 rose 15.8 per cent in the past year and FTSE 100 10.9 per cent.

 The Nikkei gained 42.1 per cent and Singapore’s Straits Times 21.7 per cent. Even Hang Seng (down 9.5 per cent) and the Shanghai Composite (down 3.1 per cent) fell less than the Nifty. 
 South Korea and Taiwan rode a chipmaker rally on artificial-intelligence (AI) demand. Samsung Electronics returned 215 per cent including dividends, SK Hynix 352 per cent and Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company 74.6 per cent. South Korea’s 10 largest companies together returned 211 per cent. 
 G Chokkalingam of Equinomics Research doubts the chip-led rally will last. “My belief is that the AI boom is not sustainable,” he said, adding that he remains positive on India over the longer term.
 “So, I am very bullish. India will have an excellent future after 3-4 years. But before that, if this war continues for 6 months, we can have one big shock,” he said.
 India’s heavyweights went the other way. Its 10 most-valuable companies returned close to minus 20 per cent, dragged by Tata Consultancy Services (down 34.5 per cent), HDFC Bank (34 per cent), Hindustan Unilever (30 per cent) and Reliance Industries (21.6 per cent).
 Only about a third of Indian largecaps in the Bloomberg sample ended the year higher, against more than four in five in South Korea and Taiwan.
 The premium India long commanded over its neighbours has narrowed, but not because companies stopped making money. Aggregate profits of Indian firms in the sample rose about 6 per cent on Bloomberg’s prior-year comparison. Investors are simply paying less for them, and putting their money where the chips are. 
 “We missed a great opportunity to stand out. India does not figure in the top 10 destinations of global investors right now,” said Abhay Agarwal, founder and fund manager, Piper Serica. According to him, the private sector and innovation by large companies should be given more government support, along with more structured reforms, policies and regulations. 
 India’s large listed companies are now worth $3.67 trillion, less than Taiwan’s $4.59 trillion and barely ahead of Korea’s $3.62 trillion. In dollar terms, the Nifty 50’s market value has shrunk 17.3 per cent in a year to $1.88 trillion.
 A February 2 trade deal cut US tariffs on Indian goods to 18 per cent from 50 per cent, but the relief lasted less than four weeks. On February 28, the US and Israeli strikes on Iran triggered a war that has since choked shipping through the Strait of Hormuz.
 For a country that imports at least 88.7 per cent of its crude, the timing could hardly have been worse. Brent, at $72 before the war, topped $104 this week. Foreign investors pulled a record ₹1.14 trillion from Indian equities in March alone. The rupee has slid to about 96.7 to the dollar, down 8.21 per cent over the past year and 7.09 per cent so far in 2026, and on Wednesday the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) raised the repo rate by 25 basis points (bps) to 5.5 per cent, its first hike since February 2023. The currency has weakened 4.21 per cent over six months and 1.39 per cent over three months, while falling 5.95 per cent since the Iran war began. The rupee also fell 0.94 per cent in the current quarter and month, and 0.44 per cent over the past week.
 South Korea and Taiwan also import at least 94 per cent of their oil, but sustained massive gain due to their stakes in the semiconductor chip boom, which gave them an edge over Indian equities.
 Valuations have fallen with prices. The Nifty trades at 20.3 times earnings, down from 23.6 a year ago, implying its companies’ earnings rose about 4 per cent even as the index fell.
 The Taiex has risen to 27.9 times from 23.1. The Kospi’s multiple has dropped to 12.1 from 16.6 despite the rally, as profits outpaced prices.
 “The biggest worry for India is that the global oil price is up, and the rupee also depreciated. Hence, the impact has doubled. The rupee has to start recovering, and only then will the foreign institutional investor (FII) money come,” said Chokkalingam.
 “To get back the confidence of global investors, we need to get back on the high growth cycle which will require coordinated effort between the government and private sector,” Agarwal added.

Datanomics: BSE took a decade to enter the Nifty 50; any lessons for NSE?
 BSE took over a decade to enter the Nifty 50, climbing from smallcap to midcap and then largecap. NSE's journey could follow a similar path
 premium 
 Image: Bloomberg
 Shreya Eswaran New Delhi 3 min read Last Updated : Oct 09 2026 | 11:55 PM IST
 Listen to This Article
 The National Stock Exchange of India (NSE) listed on its rival exchange, the BSE, on September 24 this year. It is yet to enter any major index though, given the rules and criteria that must be fulfilled for becoming eligible to enter an index. It was almost a decade ago, on February 3, 2017, when BSE was listed on NSE. Rules do not permit an exchange to list on its own platform. It took BSE over ten years to enter the Nifty 50, but its path up the index ladder was gradual: from a non-index stock to the Nifty Smallcap 100, then to the midcap index, and finally to the Nifty 50. 
 To be clear, several criteria determine a stock’s entry into any index including a stock’s listing history of at least six months. For NSE, achieving this threshold is just over five months away since it listed recently. Secondly, since benchmark indices have derivatives on it, it is also necessary that a stock is eligible and part of Futures & Options (F&O) segment before being permitted in the index. And, the stock has to meet the minimum volume, trade, and other thresholds for being eligible in F&O. Inclusion in leading benchmarks requires a stock to meet even higher standards. 
 A stock’s placement, particularly in smallcap and midcap segments, depends on its impact cost, which measures liquidity or transaction costs. A lower impact cost means the stock is highly liquid, large volumes can be bought or sold easily without significantly moving the stock price. BSE entered the Nifty Smallcap 100 over five years after its listing in April 2022, overtaking BEML. It took almost two years for BSE to move into the Nifty Midcap index by toppling Indian Renewable Energy Development Agency (IREDA). Another two-and-a-half years later, BSE found its way into the Nifty 50, replacing Wipro. BSE officially entered the Nifty 50 on September 30 this year following the semi-annual index rebalancing by NSE Indices. 
 While BSE’s entry into the smallcap and midcap indices was also linked to the size of its market capitalisaton then, NSE has already started its journey as a large cap with a market cap of ₹4.28 trillion based on Friday’s closing; BSE is currently valued at ₹1.34 trillion. 
 While it would be interesting to see how soon NSE enters a benchmark index, the journey of one of the largest exchanges globally is likely to be much shorter.

Largecaps look ripe on valuations, but flows hold back: Krishna Sanghavi
 Mahindra Manulife MF's Krishna Sangahvi says largecap valuations look attractive, but cautious domestic investors and uncertain foreign flows remain key challenges.
 premium 
 Krishna Sanghavi, CIO Equity, Mahindra Manulife Mutual Fund
 Abhishek Kumar Mumbai 4 min read Last Updated : Oct 11 2026 | 11:17 PM IST
 Listen to This Article
 Largecap valuations have turned attractive after the market correction. Still, a revival in foreign investor flows remains
 uncertain amid currency risks and continued capital flight from emerging markets (EMs), says Krishna Sanghavi , chief investment officer — equity, Mahindra Manulife Mutual Fund (MF). In an interaction with Abhishek Kumar in Mumbai, he discusses his sectoral preferences, mid and smallcap valuations, and shortening market cycles. Edited excerpts : 
 Oil prices have remained elevated for several months now. To what extent do you think Indian equities already price in these risks? 
 We believe this needs to be viewed from the perspective of two different sets of investors — domestic and global. From the perspective of domestic investors, a significant part of the risk is probably already priced in. Oil prices have remained elevated for more than six months, so the macroeconomic impact of higher energy prices has already been factored into market expectations to some extent. 
 The situation is somewhat different for global investors. For them, it is not just about the impact of higher oil prices on the Indian economy but also about currency movements and returns in dollar terms. Arguably, the bigger impact of the current situation has been felt through the currency. 
 There is also a broader EM angle. India is not the only market seeing foreign investor outflows. A sizeable amount of global capital has moved towards US markets over the past several quarters, while the EM basket has come under pressure. 
 Largecaps have corrected the most since the flare-up in West Asia. Has the segment turned attractive? 
 From a valuation perspective, largecaps look attractive as a basket. However, flows remain a challenge. If global investors remain cautious about EMs, foreign portfolio investor selling will continue to weigh on India. This creates a meaningful near-term headwind for largecaps, even when valuations look reasonable. 
 Interestingly, domestic investors are also becoming somewhat more cautious about largecaps, while continuing to allocate relatively more capital to mid and smallcaps.
 Are continued strong domestic flows into mid and smallcap stocks raising valuation concerns? 
 It is difficult to take a blanket view on mid and smallcaps because there is considerable dispersion within these segments. Midcaps are somewhat different. The universe is much more restricted, and the limited number of eligible companies can itself create a valuation premium when flows are strong. 
 In smallcaps, one important development is the widening of the investable universe. Once you move beyond the top 250 stocks, the number of potential opportunities expands. However, rich valuations mean investors need to look much further ahead. Many smallcap companies are now talking about their growth plans for 2030-31 and beyond. Investing in this segment, therefore, increasingly requires a longer investment horizon rather than a focus solely on the next 18-24 months. 
 From a sectoral perspective, where do you see the strongest opportunities in India? 
 India remains a growth economy, with nominal growth potentially in the 10-11 per cent range, offering opportunities across several sectors. The challenge is increasingly about valuations and timing rather than simply identifying sectors with growth potential. 
 One structural theme that stands out is manufacturing. The post-pandemic global environment has encouraged companies and countries to diversify their supply chains. India could potentially benefit from this shift. 
 The government’s efforts to expand its network of free trade agreements and promote import substitution also support the domestic manufacturing ecosystem.The caveat is that market cycles have become much shorter. A sector can move sharply once the market starts recognising the theme, but the resulting valuation cycle can also run its course quickly. 
 How do you manage portfolios in such an environment? 
 The core approach remains to focus on companies whose underlying business models and earnings trajectories are intact and whose governance is not a concern. A portfolio need not exit a company completely simply because its stock has become expensive. Instead, valuations can be managed through position sizing. 
 The other important factor is sector rotation. Even if a company’s fundamentals remain strong, global sector allocations may change, creating opportunities elsewhere. Portfolio management, therefore, increasingly requires tracking both company-level earnings dynamics and the broader market’s changing preferences. 
 This is particularly important because sector cycles are now much shorter. A sector may deliver its returns over a relatively compressed period and then enter a phase of time correction rather than necessarily undergoing a sharp price correction.

Street signs: IPO activity set to regain momentum, new MF schemes slow
 IPOs, technical indicators and mutual fund launches offer a snapshot of primary market activity amid equity market volatility
 premium 
 Four companies are set to announce IPO price bands, while technical indicators suggest a possible Nifty relief rally and volatile markets delay mutual fund scheme launches. | Representative Image
 Shilpa Rangarajan Abhishek Kumar Mumbai / New Delhi 2 min read Last Updated : Oct 11 2026 | 10:57 PM IST
 Listen to This Article
 Primary market activity is set to resume after a brief lull, as at least four companies are set to announce their initial public offering (IPO) price bands on Monday. Bonfiglioli Transmissions, Zetwerk Manufacturing Business, Tonbo Imaging, and Sahajanand Medical Technologies will announce their IPO price bands, with Zetwerk alone planning to raise ₹5,000 crore through its IPO. Zetwerk is a mixed bag of fresh issues and an offer for sale (OFS), meanwhile Tonbo Imaging, Bonfiglioli and Sahajanand are 
 entirely OFS IPOs, according to their latest publicly available filings. Investors will have to brace for caution as OFS IPOs especially of large sizes have shown underperformance amid turbulent secondary markets after listing. 
 Glimmer of hope in technical indicators 
 After a long correction spell, technical indicators offer a glimmer of recovery hope for the Nifty 50, with a weekly Doji formation raising the possibility of a relief rally, according to Osho Krishan, chief manager — technical and derivative research at Angel One. However, the broader trend remains weak, with 22,000-22,200 emerging as a crucial support zone. Separately, Choice Institutional Equities said Nifty’s recovery after briefly slipping below the previous low of 22,182.55 indicates buying interest at lower levels. The index remains below its 50-week Exponential Moving Average (EMA), while the 200-week EMA near 22,382 remains a key technical reference. 
 New MF schemes slow as market turns volatile 
 New scheme launches by mutual funds have hit the slow lane in October amid market turbulence. Only four new fund offerings (NFOs) have hit the market this month even as fund houses have approvals. More than 40 mutual fund schemes were filed with the Securities and Exchange Board of India (Sebi) in September. While some have already been launched, several are yet to hit the market. Fund houses have flexibility to defer launches, with Sebi allowing schemes to be launched within six months of its final observations. This could give asset managers room to wait for more stable market conditions before launching new equity-oriented schemes. According to industry insiders, with the 15-day inauspicious Pitru Paksha period now over, the launches are expected to pick up.

Sebi to issue closing auction guidelines in a week: Tuhin Kanta Pandey
 The regulator is also working to simplify digital onboarding for persons resident outside India (PROIs), allowing them to access Indian markets without requiring their physical presence
 Tuhin Kanta Pandey, chairman, Securities and Exchange Board of India (Sebi). (File Photo - Credit: Kamlesh Pednekar)
 Khushboo Tiwari Mumbai 2 min read Last Updated : Oct 10 2026 | 7:28 PM IST
 Listen to This Article
 The Securities and Exchange Board of India (Sebi) is examining comments received on its consultation paper on the Closing Auction Session (CAS) and may issue guidelines in about a week, chairman Tuhin Kanta Pandey said on Saturday. 
 The consultation paper was aimed at addressing concerns regarding the settlement price of derivatives on expiry days and had received over 20,000 comments from traders and industry stakeholders. 
 The regulator is also working to simplify digital onboarding for persons resident outside India (PROIs), allowing them to access Indian markets without requiring their physical presence. Sebi has received more than 400 comments on the proposal and will issue a circular shortly, Pandey said at the second Capital Market Confluence organised by the Bombay Stock Exchange Brokers’ Forum in Mumbai. 
 Separately, the regulator is exploring a graded compliance framework for stock brokers based on their scale, client exposure and technology dependence, as part of efforts to make regulation simpler and more proportionate. 
 Sebi is also targeting the end of November to bring certain transactions, including tender offers, buybacks and offers for sale, within the interoperability framework. These transactions currently require parallel clearing arrangements, increasing costs and compliance requirements, Pandey said.

 The proposed changes are expected to improve capital efficiency and reduce compliance costs while preserving settlement safety.
 He highlighted recent regulatory measures, including the rationalisation of penalties for stock brokers across exchanges, changes to the technical-glitch framework and the introduction of a common, principle-based advertisement code for specified Sebi-regulated entities. 
 The regulator is also reviewing the Depositories and Participants Regulations to simplify rules and strengthen fraud prevention.
 On technology, Pandey said Sebi would shortly issue guidelines for the responsible use of artificial intelligence and machine learning. These would follow a tiered approach, with clear accountability, data controls, kill switches and human oversight.

docs.text: HDFC Bank, Tata Consultancy Services (TCS) and Titan Company have received ‘Buy’ ratings from multiple brokerages, with analysts citing leadership stability, technology spending and consumer demand as key factors shaping their outlooks. HDFC Bank’s recommendations point to scope for better execution and profitability. For TCS, analysts are watching deal conversion and demand for artificial intelligence services. Titan’s expanding retail network and growth across consumer businesses support its outlook, although jewellery sales have fallen short of some estimates. HDFC Bank Emkay Global Financial Services Emkay Global has a ‘Buy’ on HDFC Bank and a target price of Rs 1,225, implying potential upside of 69.9%. The brokerage’s positive view follows regulatory approval for Anup Bagchi’s appointment as managing director and chief executive officer. Leadership stability is expected to help the bank maintain its strategic priorities and improve execution. Deposit mobilisation, branch productivity and digital capabilities are central to Emkay’s assessment. The bank’s ability to strengthen its deposit base while improving operating performance will be important to earnings growth. The target price also reflects the brokerage’s view that better execution could support a higher valuation. Motilal Oswal Financial Services Motilal Oswal has a ‘Buy’ rating on HDFC Bank and a target price of Rs 925, indicating potential upside of 28.3%. ALSO READIndia’s FII paradox: $9.2 billion into IPOs, $39 billion pulled from listed stocks The brokerage expects leadership clarity to help the bank maintain its operating priorities and improve performance over time. Its outlook factors in a gradual recovery in profitability, with return on assets estimated at around 1.7%. Motilal Oswal expects the loan book to grow at a compound annual rate of roughly 14% between FY26 and FY28. Loan growth, deposit mobilisation and a stronger contribution from core banking operations will be important to achieving that forecast. The recommendation rests on the bank’s ability to translate its scale and franchise strength into improved returns. Jefferies Jefferies too has a ‘Buy’ rating on HDFC Bank and a target price of Rs 880, implying potential upside of around 19.6%. The brokerage’s assessment focuses on the leadership transition and the bank’s ability to sustain execution. Consistent progress on its operating priorities could help improve confidence in the bank’s performance. Retail deposit growth, fee income and the composition of the loan book are also important to Jefferies’ outlook. Funding costs and the loan mix can influence margins and returns, making continued improvement in these areas central to the brokerage’s positive view. Tata Consultancy Services Nomura Nomura has rated TCS ‘Buy’ with a target price of Rs 2,630, implying potential upside of around 20.6%. ALSO READ5 Penny Stocks Under Rs 100 to Watch for Long-Term Growth The brokerage’s outlook accounts for continued scrutiny of discretionary technology spending and project timelines. Nomura has reduced its FY27 earnings-per-share forecast by 2.6%, while leaving its FY28 forecast unchanged. Some projects have been deferred, although the brokerage expects the affected work could return over the medium term. Artificial intelligence remains an important growth opportunity for TCS, with AI-related services accounting for around 10% of revenue. As clients invest in automation and technology transformation, the company has an opportunity to expand its role in these projects. The pace at which demand converts into revenue will be important to its growth outlook. Motilal Oswal Financial Services Motilal Oswal Financial Services has a ‘Buy’ rating on TCS and a target price of Rs 2,400, indicating potential upside of around 10.1%. The brokerage has pointed to total contract value of US$9.6 billion as evidence of continued deal activity. However, contract wins need to translate into revenue, making the conversion of the sales pipeline an important factor in the near-term outlook. Motilal Oswal’s assessment also depends on a recovery in regional demand and stronger conversion of client discussions into projects. Technology modernisation and AI-led transformation work could support growth, although the timing of client spending remains an important consideration.
